title: Python basics
summary: What a program is, how Python stores values, and how to write your first function.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.objective: Understand variable declaration, identifier rules, and value reassignment.
lessons.explanation: In Python, variables are labels bound to objects in memory. You do not declare types explicitly. Assignment is performed using '='.

lessons.title: Data Types
lessons.objective: Distinguish between numeric and text data types and cast between them.
lessons.explanation: Python features built-in types such as int, float, str, and bool. The type() function inspects an object's type, and constructor functions like int() or str() perform conversion.

title: Variables, input/output and operators
summary: Reading input, printing output, and doing arithmetic and comparisons.

lessons.title: Input and Output
lessons.objective: Format output strings accurately using f-strings and understand string templating.
lessons.explanation: Output is printed using print(). F-strings (f'...') provide concise, readable interpolation of expressions directly within string literals.

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.objective: Apply operator precedence and boolean logic effectively.
lessons.explanation: Arithmetic includes +, -, *, /, // (floor div), % (modulo), and ** (power). Comparison includes ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. Logical operators are and, or, not.

title: Conditionals
summary: Making decisions in code with if, elif and else.

lessons.title: If Statements
lessons.objective: Execute code blocks conditionally when a predicate evaluates to True.
lessons.explanation: The 'if' statement evaluates a conditional expression. If the expression evaluates to True, the indented block of code runs.

lessons.title: If / Else
lessons.objective: Handle mutually exclusive logic paths.
lessons.explanation: An 'if...else' construct executes one block when the condition is True, and the alternative block when it is False.

lessons.title: If / Elif / Else
lessons.objective: Evaluate sequential conditions with a default fallback.
lessons.explanation: The 'elif' clause allows testing multiple expressions in sequence until one evaluates to True. The optional 'else' clause catches any remaining cases.

examples.title: Letter Grade

lessons.title: Nested Conditions
lessons.objective: Manage multi-tiered logical constraints with clean indentation.
lessons.explanation: Conditions placed inside other conditional blocks allow nuanced evaluation of dependent criteria.

title: Loops
summary: Repeating work with for and while, and controlling when loops stop.

lessons.title: For Loops
lessons.objective: Use range() and iterate over sequences efficiently.
lessons.explanation: A for loop iterates over each item in an iterable sequence (such as a list, string, or range) in order.

examples.title: Sum with Range

lessons.title: While Loops
lessons.objective: Implement iteration that repeats until a state condition is met.
lessons.explanation: A while loop repeats its body as long as its condition remains True. State must be updated within the loop to avoid infinite loops.

lessons.title: Break
lessons.objective: Exit loops immediately when an early stopping criterion is satisfied.
lessons.explanation: The 'break' statement terminates the innermost loop immediately, jumping execution to the first statement outside the loop.

examples.title: Early Exit

lessons.title: Continue
lessons.objective: Bypass the remainder of a loop body for specific elements.
lessons.explanation: The 'continue' statement stops execution of the current iteration and jumps directly to the next iteration of the loop.

examples.title: Skip Evens

title: Functions
summary: Packaging logic into reusable functions, parameters and return values.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.objective: Organize code into callable abstractions.
lessons.explanation: Functions group reusable logic under a name. They are defined using the 'def' keyword and invoked with parentheses.

lessons.title: Parameters
lessons.objective: Design flexible function signatures.
lessons.explanation: Parameters define values expected by a function. Default arguments assign fallback values when an argument is omitted during invocation.

examples.title: Default Parameter
examples.code:
def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

lessons.title: Return Values
lessons.objective: Send computed results back to the caller cleanly.
lessons.explanation: The 'return' statement exits a function and hands the specified value back to the caller. Omitting return implicitly returns None.

lessons.title: Scope
lessons.objective: Understand variable resolution order and lexical closures.
lessons.explanation: Python resolves variables via LEGB: Local first, then Enclosing (closure), Global (module level), and Built-in.

examples.title: Closure Counter

lessons.title: Lambda Functions
lessons.objective: Write concise inline callables for sorting and transformations.
lessons.explanation: Lambda expressions provide a syntax for anonymous functions: lambda args: expression. They are restricted to a single evaluated expression.

lessons.title: map()
lessons.objective: Utilize functional programming mappings across collections.
lessons.explanation: map(function, iterable) yields items resulting from applying the function to each element of the iterable.

lessons.title: filter()
lessons.objective: Extract subsets of collections lazily using predicate functions.
lessons.explanation: filter(predicate, iterable) extracts elements for which the predicate returns True.

title: Strings
summary: Working with text: indexing, slicing and common methods.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.objective: Access characters via 0-based and negative indexing.
lessons.explanation: Strings in Python are immutable text sequences. Character elements can be indexed using bracket syntax, e.g., text[0] or text[-1].

lessons.title: String Methods
lessons.objective: Manipulate and sanitize text using standard string methods.
lessons.explanation: Strings provide helper methods such as .lower(), .upper(), .strip(), .replace(), and .split(). Since strings are immutable, methods return a new string.

lessons.title: Slicing
lessons.objective: Extract sub-lists and reverse sequences with step values.
lessons.explanation: Sequence slicing syntax [start:stop:step] extracts a portion of a sequence. Negative steps iterate backwards (e.g. [::-1] reverses).

title: Lists and dictionaries
summary: The everyday collections: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries.

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.objective: Construct, read, and mutate list collections.
lessons.explanation: Lists are mutable sequences defined using brackets: [item1, item2]. Elements can be modified in place: items[0] = new_value.

lessons.title: List Methods
lessons.objective: Mutate lists using in-place methods vs returning new lists.
lessons.explanation: .append(x) adds an item to the end, .pop() removes and returns an item, and .sort() orders the list in place.

lessons.title: Tuples
lessons.objective: Utilize tuples for fixed-structure data records and unpacking.
lessons.explanation: Tuples are immutable sequences created using parentheses: (a, b). They are hashable (can be dict keys) and prevent accidental modification.

lessons.title: Sets
lessons.objective: Execute set operations (union, intersection, difference) for O(1) membership.
lessons.explanation: Sets store distinct hashable elements. They provide mathematical operations such as union (|), intersection (&), and difference (-).

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.objective: Map unique keys to values and access values in O(1) average time.
lessons.explanation: Dictionaries store key-value associations: {key: value}. Keys must be immutable and hashable; values can be any object.

lessons.title: Dictionary Methods
lessons.objective: Use safe key retrieval with defaults and iterate over key-value pairs.
lessons.explanation: dict.get(key, default) avoids KeyError when a key may be absent. .items() yields (key, value) pairs during iteration.

lessons.title: List Comprehensions
lessons.objective: Write readable, idiomatic one-line list transformations.
lessons.explanation: List comprehensions follow the form: [expression for item in iterable if condition]. They are faster and more concise than manual append loops.

examples.title: Squares of Evens
examples.code: evens = [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]

lessons.title: Dictionary Comprehensions
lessons.objective: Transform key-value mappings declaratively.
lessons.explanation: Dict comprehensions allow constructing dictionaries in one expression: {key_expr: val_expr for item in iterable if condition}.

examples.title: Word Lengths
examples.code:
words = ['cat', 'elephant']
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in words}

title: Recursion
summary: Solving a problem by solving a smaller version of itself.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.objective: Formulate divide-and-conquer logic with sound base cases.
lessons.explanation: A recursive function calls itself to solve smaller sub-problems. Every recursive function must define a base case to terminate execution.

examples.title: Factorial
examples.code:
def fact(n):
    return 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1)

title: Searching and sorting
summary: Finding and ordering data, and reasoning about how long it takes.

lessons.title: Searching
lessons.objective: Implement binary search and recognize when sorted order enables logarithmic time.
lessons.explanation: Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted search interval in half. Comparing the target with the middle element eliminates half the candidates.

examples.title: Binary Search
examples.code:
def bin_search(arr, x):
    low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1

lessons.title: Sorting
lessons.objective: Understand in-place vs out-of-place sorting and stability.
lessons.explanation: Sorting orders elements according to a comparator. Bubble sort swaps adjacent inverted pairs; merge sort divides and merges sorted halves in O(n log n).

lessons.title: Algorithmic Complexity / Big-O
lessons.objective: Analyze asymptotic upper bounds and select optimal data structures.
lessons.explanation: Big-O notation describes how execution time or space requirements scale asymptotically as the input size n approaches infinity.

examples.title: Comparing Complexities
examples.code: # O(1) hash lookup vs O(n) linear search

title: Arrays and two pointers
summary: Walking through arrays with two indices and sliding windows.

lessons.title: Two-pointer Problems
lessons.objective: Optimize linear sequence problems from O(n^2) to O(n) using pointer convergence.
lessons.explanation: Two pointers iterate from both ends toward each other or travel at different speeds to solve partitioned array problems in a single pass.

examples.title: Two Pointer Palindrome
examples.code:
left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
while left < right:
    if s[left] != s[right]: return False
    left += 1; right -= 1
return True

lessons.title: Sliding windows
lessons.explanation: To examine consecutive ranges, update the previous result instead of recomputing it. Add the value entering the window and subtract the one leaving.

title: Hashing
summary: Trading memory for speed with dictionaries and sets.

lessons.title: Hash-map Problems
lessons.objective: Trade space for time by caching seen elements in a hash map.
lessons.explanation: Hash maps provide O(1) expected time key lookups. By storing complements or previously seen elements, quadratic brute-force searches can be reduced to linear time.

examples.title: Two Sum with Map

lessons.title: Why dictionaries are fast
lessons.explanation: Looking up a key in a dict or set takes about the same time however large it grows. Many nested-loop solutions become single loops by remembering what you have already seen.

title: Stacks and queues
summary: Last-in first-out and first-in first-out structures.

lessons.title: Stack
lessons.objective: Utilize stacks for undo mechanisms, syntax parsing, and depth-first traversals.
lessons.explanation: A stack enforces LIFO ordering. Elements are added with push/append and removed from the top with pop().

examples.title: Balanced Parentheses

lessons.title: Queue
lessons.objective: Model sequential service buffers using collections.deque.
lessons.explanation: A queue enforces FIFO ordering. Elements are inserted at the back and removed from the front.

examples.title: Queue with Deque
examples.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append(1)
first = q.popleft()

title: Linked lists
summary: Chains of nodes connected by references, and pointer techniques.

lessons.title: Nodes and references
lessons.explanation: A linked list stores each value in a node that also holds a reference to the next node. Moving through the list means following those references, so keep track of which node you are on and be careful not to lose the rest of the chain when you change a reference.

examples.title: Walking a list
examples.code:
node = head
while node is not None:
    print(node.val)
    node = node.next

lessons.title: Fast and slow pointers
lessons.explanation: Moving one reference two steps for every one step of another finds the middle of a list and detects cycles, using almost no extra memory.

title: Trees
summary: Hierarchical data, traversals and binary search trees.

lessons.title: Binary trees
lessons.explanation: A binary tree node has a value and up to two children. Most tree problems become simple when you ask what to do at one node, and let recursion handle the subtrees.

examples.title: Counting nodes

lessons.title: Binary search trees
lessons.explanation: In a binary search tree, smaller values are on the left and larger values are on the right, so each comparison lets you ignore a whole subtree.

title: Graphs
summary: Networks of nodes, breadth-first and depth-first search.

lessons.title: Representing graphs
lessons.explanation: An adjacency list maps each node to its neighbours. In Python, a dictionary of lists works well.

lessons.title: Breadth-first and depth-first search
lessons.explanation: Search visits nodes while remembering which were already seen, so cycles cannot trap you. A queue explores level by level, which gives the fewest steps. A stack or recursion explores deeply.

lessons.title: Overlapping subproblems
lessons.explanation: If a recursive solution computes the same smaller answer many times, store each answer the first time. That turns exponential work into something practical.

examples.title: Memoization

lessons.title: Building a table
lessons.explanation: You can also fill answers from smallest to largest in a list. First define in words what each entry means, then how it depends on earlier entries.

title: Python toolkit (optional)
summary: Optional extras: exceptions, modules, classes, iterators and generators.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.objective: Catch specific runtime errors and maintain program stability.
lessons.explanation: Exceptions signal runtime errors. A try-except block allows intercepting expected errors (e.g. ValueError, ZeroDivisionError) gracefully.

examples.title: Safe Division

lessons.title: File Handling
lessons.objective: Manage I/O streams and guarantee resource disposal via context managers.
lessons.explanation: The 'with open(path, mode)' statement manages file streams and automatically closes them when the block exits, even if exceptions occur.

examples.title: Read Lines
examples.code:
with open('data.txt', 'r') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

lessons.title: Modules
lessons.objective: Import and reuse modular functions from the Python Standard Library.
lessons.explanation: A module is a Python file containing executable code and definitions. Modules are loaded with 'import module_name'.

lessons.title: Packages
lessons.objective: Structure multi-file Python applications into packages.
lessons.explanation: Packages are directory structures that group related modules, providing dotted module names.

lessons.title: Classes
lessons.objective: Model real-world entities using object-oriented abstractions.
lessons.explanation: Classes serve as blueprints for objects. Methods defined inside a class accept 'self' as their first argument referring to the instance.

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.objective: Manipulate instance state and call instance methods.
lessons.explanation: An object is a concrete instance of a class, possessing its own unique attribute values.

lessons.title: Constructors
lessons.objective: Set up instance attributes during instantiation.
lessons.explanation: The __init__ method is invoked automatically when a new instance is created to set initial attributes.

examples.title: Constructor

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.objective: Derive specialized child classes from common parent abstractions.
lessons.explanation: Inheritance enables a child class to inherit attributes and methods from a parent class, using super() to invoke parent behaviors.

examples.title: Subclass

lessons.title: Iterators
lessons.objective: Implement custom stream iterators following Python's protocol.
lessons.explanation: An iterator is an object that implements __iter__() (returning self) and __next__() (returning the next value or raising StopIteration).

examples.title: Iterator Protocol

lessons.title: Generators
lessons.objective: Construct memory-efficient data streams.
lessons.explanation: Generators are functions that yield values one at a time using 'yield', suspending and resuming their state between calls.

examples.title: Fibonacci Generator
